content.title: Are air traffic controllers part of the government shutdown?
content.text: NEW YORK (PIX11) — A TSA staffing shortage and a deadly plane crash at LaGuardia Airport have raised fresh questions about air traffic controller staffing as the partial government shutdown continues. The crash, which killed two pilots and injured multiple people, has also renewed scrutiny of the FAA, an agency that has faced questions over staffing, oversight and safety practices in recent years. However, FAA officials say controllers’ pay and operations remain unaffected by the shutdown. Air traffic controllers work for the Federal Aviation Administration, which is part of the Department of Transportation. The FAA is fully funded for fiscal year 2026, according to FAA officials. The partial government shutdown failed to renew funding for the Department of Homeland Security, which includes the TSA, U.S. Secret Service, and Coast Guard. Both TSA officers and air traffic controllers are considered essential and continue reporting to work during a shutdown. However, the partial government shutdown prompted 400 TSA officers to quit, and thousands more have called out sick because they’re not getting paid. Government shutdowns, however, can delay the hiring and training of new FAA personnel, according to an FAA workforce plan covering 2025 through 2028. While the FAA remains funded and controllers continue to work during the shutdown, the agency’s workforce plan warns that any disruption to hiring and training could have long‑term effects. LaGuardia has a target staffing level of 37 air traffic controllers, with 33 currently employed and seven in training, officials said Monday at a news conference on the plane crash. The agency anticipates losing 6,872 controllers through 2028, though the overall workforce is still expected to grow, according to the same report.
